subtype: Stage 3: A cold reply, a colder one [Actor]
passage: Okay, so, I'm Tanvir, and you asked why I've been grumpy all morning. Last night I got off a twelve-hour shift and texted my wife, Damini: 'Picking up dinner, what do you want?' She'd had her own awful day, apparently. She replied, 'fine.' Just 'fine.' To a question about dinner! I was so tired I typed, 'what is your problem?' and hit send before I'd even read it. She wrote back, 'my problem is you.' So I wrote, 'great, very mature.' She sent 'ok.' with a full stop. That full stop felt like a slap. By the time I got home with biryani nobody wanted, we weren't speaking. The stupid part? I don't think either of us was angry about dinner. We were just two exhausted people answering each other's tone.

qa.q: What did Tanvir text Damini after his shift?
qa.a: 'Picking up dinner, what do you want?'

qa.q: Why did Tanvir send 'what is your problem?' without rereading it?
qa.a: He was exhausted after a twelve-hour shift and reacted to the flat tone of 'fine' rather than to what Damini actually meant.

qa.q: At which point could Tanvir have stopped the escalation, and how?
qa.a: Right after 'fine', he could have asked, 'Rough day? I'll just bring your usual,' answering her likely tiredness instead of her tone.

qa.q: What might Damini have been feeling when she replied 'fine'?
qa.a: She'd had an awful day and was probably too drained to think about dinner, not angry at Tanvir, until his reply made her feel attacked.

grounding: A tired husband describes his wife's 'fine' and his 'what is your problem?' escalating into colder lines, each answering tone rather than intent.

subtype: Stage 3: A cold reply, a colder one [Actor]
passage: I'm Hrithik. Tejas and I were at the tea stall after cricket when his phone buzzed. He read it and his jaw went tight. 'What?' I asked. He showed me: he'd written, 'Coming home by nine, need anything?' and his wife, Nupur, had replied, 'fine.' He typed fast: 'what is your problem?' Sent. Her reply came in seconds; I only saw his face drop. He typed again, harder, thumbs stabbing the screen. This went on for ten minutes, each message shorter than the last. His tea went cold. I don't know what Nupur was thinking; maybe she'd had a long day too. But from where I sat, they weren't arguing about anything. They were just answering each other's tone.

qa.q: What had Tejas written to Nupur?
qa.a: 'Coming home by nine, need anything?'

qa.q: What do Tejas's stabbing thumbs suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt irritated and stung by the flat 'fine', and his anger rose with each short reply.

qa.q: What could Hrithik say to Tejas to help break the loop?
qa.a: He could suggest Tejas stop typing and call Nupur, or just ask about her day, since the texts are escalating over tone, not a real issue.

qa.q: Why might Nupur have replied with just 'fine'?
qa.a: As Hrithik guesses, she may have been tired after a long day and meant nothing harsh, then felt attacked by 'what is your problem?'

grounding: A friend watches a husband answer his wife's 'fine' with 'what is your problem?', and both escalate over tone rather than intention.

subtype: Stage 4: Family or friends pulled in [Observer]
passage: Darshan, you're newly married, so let your Urmila Nani tell you something I watched with my own eyes. When your mother was twenty-five, she had a silly text fight with your father, something about who forgot the gas bill. She phoned her sister, your Meenu Masi, from my verandah. I was shelling peas nearby. Meenu listened for two minutes and said, 'He always does this. Always. Don't let him treat you like that.' I watched your mother's face change. Before the call she was annoyed. After it, she was certain. It wasn't about a gas bill any more; it was about what kind of man he was. Meenu meant well; she loved her sister. But she'd heard only one side.

qa.q: What was Urmila doing while her daughter was on the phone?
qa.a: She was shelling peas nearby.

qa.q: How did the mother's feelings change during the call with Meenu?
qa.a: She went from mildly annoyed to angrily certain, as Meenu's 'he always does this' turned a small quarrel into a judgement of her husband.

qa.q: What could Meenu have said instead that would have helped?
qa.a: She could have listened, asked what he said about it, and suggested talking to him directly, rather than giving a verdict on hearing one side.

qa.q: How might Darshan's father have experienced that evening?
qa.a: He probably came home to a wife far angrier than a gas bill deserved, without knowing a verdict about him had been reached in his absence.

grounding: A grandmother recalls watching her daughter vent to her sister, whose 'he always does this' turned a small text quarrel into a settled verdict.

subtype: Stage 4: Family or friends pulled in [Observer]
passage: The cab had not moved for twenty minutes on the flooded road, rain drumming on the roof, and Salma's phone was on four per cent. Elizabeth, squeezed beside her, couldn't help hearing. Salma had her sister on speaker. 'Imran just sent "fine, suit yourself" when I said I'd be late. Who does that?' Her sister's voice crackled back: 'He always does this, Salma. Remember Eid? Remember your birthday? He doesn't respect you.' Elizabeth watched Salma's jaw set. 'You're right,' Salma said. 'I'm done being nice.' The phone died. Salma stared out at the brake lights, arms crossed. Elizabeth had no idea what Imran was like. But she'd noticed that ten minutes ago Salma had sounded tired, and now she sounded sure.

qa.q: How much battery was left on Salma's phone?
qa.a: Salma's phone was on four per cent.

qa.q: How did Salma's feelings shift during the call, as Elizabeth saw it?
qa.a: Salma went from sounding tired to sounding sure and angry, as her sister's 'he always does this' hardened her view of Imran.

qa.q: What might have helped Salma more than her sister's verdict?
qa.a: Waiting until she was home and calmer, then asking Imran what he meant, before letting one-sided advice decide how she felt.

qa.q: What might Imran be thinking while Salma's phone is dead?
qa.a: He may have no idea how his short text landed or that a verdict is forming about him, and might be worried when her phone goes silent.

grounding: Stuck in flooded traffic, a colleague hears a woman's sister say 'he always does this' and watches a passing quarrel become a settled verdict.

passage:
Supervisor's notebook, Ramesh, Thursday.
During the vendor review, Jatin's phone kept buzzing face down. At the break he asked to step out for five minutes. I was in the corridor and heard him call his wife, Mitali. His voice was low and steady: 'I was rushed and my message sounded harsh. Farooq is in hospital; I was trying to arrange things between slides. I'm sorry.' A pause. Then he laughed a little and said, 'Yes, I'll eat something.' He came back in looking lighter.
What I did next: told him to leave at four and go to the hospital; I'd cover the last agenda item. Also noted for myself: explaining the context and owning the tone ended it in under two minutes. Worth remembering at home.

qa.q: Who is in hospital, according to Jatin?
qa.a: Farooq is in hospital.

qa.q: What does Jatin coming back 'looking lighter' suggest?
qa.a: He felt relieved after clearing things up with Mitali, no longer carrying the tension of a harsh message left unexplained.

qa.q: What made Jatin's call end the loop so quickly?
qa.a: He owned his harsh tone, gave the real context of a friend in hospital, and apologised, so Mitali didn't have to guess his intention.

qa.q: How might Mitali have felt hearing the call?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and softened once she knew why the message was harsh, which may be why she told him to eat something.

grounding: A supervisor overhears a husband step out to explain that he was rushed, a friend is in hospital, and apologise, ending the text loop fast.

passage:
Friday, 11 p.m.
This afternoon Anup texted 'can't talk. later.' after I sent him the tile photos for the bathroom. I told Swati, and she said, 'Classic Anup.' By five I'd written three angry replies in my head.
Then at six he called from outside his office, traffic honking behind him. 'Neelu, I was rushed and that sounded harsh. Bala's in hospital; I was on the phone with his family. I'm sorry.' Just like that. I felt all the heat drain out of me. I asked about Bala. He asked about the tiles. We even laughed about the ugly blue ones.
Note to self: two minutes of context fixed what three hours of guessing made worse. Also, maybe don't call Swati first.
- Neelam

qa.q: What did Anup text after seeing the tile photos?
qa.a: 'can't talk. later.'

qa.q: What does 'all the heat drain out' tell us about Neelam's feelings during the call?
qa.a: Neelam's anger melted into relief once the real reason, a friend in hospital, and an apology were given.

qa.q: What lesson does Neelam draw, and why is it useful?
qa.a: That a little context fixes what guessing makes worse, and that checking with the person before venting to others can stop a small quarrel from growing.

qa.q: What might Anup have been feeling when he called from outside his office?
qa.a: He was likely stressed about Bala and worried that his short text had hurt, wanting to clear it up quickly.

grounding: A diary records a husband calling to say he was rushed, a friend is in hospital and he is sorry, which dissolves hours of guessing.

subtype: Stage 6: Agreed norms for hard topics [Response]
passage: Darshan's night shifts at the hospital pharmacy meant he and Urmila overlapped for barely two hours a day, and most of their marriage happened by text. After last month's week-long sulk over a message that turned out to mean nothing, they sat on the balcony one Sunday and wrote two rules on a sticky note for the fridge. One: anything emotional waits for the 8 p.m. call before his shift, or Sunday breakfast. Two: if a text feels curt, the reply is a question, not a verdict. The test came on Wednesday. Darshan texted, 'Can't. Busy.' Urmila felt the old sting. Then she remembered who had written it: the man who left her tea in a flask every morning. She typed, 'All ok? 🤍' He replied an hour later: 'Sorry! Emergency order. Love you.'

qa.q: When does anything emotional get discussed, according to their first rule?
qa.a: It waits for the 8 p.m. call before his shift, or Sunday breakfast.

qa.q: Why was Urmila able to move past 'the old sting' on Wednesday?
qa.a: She remembered Darshan's loving intent, the man who left her tea in a flask every morning, and chose to read his text generously.

qa.q: Why do these two rules suit a couple with so little overlap?
qa.a: They keep hard feelings for moments when voices and time are available, and turn curt texts into questions, so busy-hour messages don't snowball.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel reading Urmila's question during an emergency?
qa.a: He probably feels cared for rather than accused, which makes it easy to explain and apologise once he's free.

grounding: A couple with clashing shifts agree that emotional talk goes to a call and a curt text gets a question, and the wife reads a short text with generosity.

subtype: Stage 6: Agreed norms for hard topics [Response]
passage: On the first Sunday of every month, Francis and Ankita had a ritual at the dining table of their Panaji flat: filter coffee, and a look back at the month's texts. Today Ankita scrolled to a Tuesday message of hers: 'do what you want.' Francis grinned. 'And I replied?' '"What does that mean?"' she read. 'Question, not a fight. Rule two.' They'd agreed on the rules after a bad spring: anything that hurt or mattered went to a phone call or the evening walk, never a paragraph over chat. And a short text got a question before a reaction. 'I was only exhausted that day,' Ankita said. 'I know,' said Francis. 'You love me too much to mean that.' She threw a cushion at him, laughing.

qa.q: What did Francis reply to 'do what you want'?
qa.a: 'What does that mean?'

qa.q: What does Francis's line 'You love me too much to mean that' show about how he reads Ankita?
qa.a: He reads her with generosity, remembering her love and intent rather than taking the curt words at face value.

qa.q: What makes their monthly look-back a useful habit?
qa.a: It lets them notice misreadings calmly, laugh at them, and keep practising their rules before small snowballs grow.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt on Tuesday when Francis asked instead of reacting?
qa.a: Probably relieved 😊, since her exhaustion was met with a question rather than a fight.

grounding: A couple review their texts monthly, keeping emotional topics for calls or walks and meeting curt texts with questions, reading each other generously.

passage: I'm Chaitanya, the helper in Pradeep sir's nursery class. Gunjan came back on Monday, a week after her Dada died. She ran straight to the sand tray and built a castle, laughing, as if nothing had happened. Then at colouring time her red crayon snapped. She sobbed and sobbed, face in her arms. Pradeep sir knelt beside her. 'You're very sad. I'm here.' He gave her a new crayon and kept the day's routine the same. By snack time she was playing again.

qa.q: What did Gunjan build when she came back?
qa.a: She built a castle in the sand tray.

qa.q: Why might a snapped crayon make Gunjan sob so hard?
qa.a: Her big sadness about Dada may come out in short bursts, and a small loss like a crayon can let it spill over.

qa.q: What did Pradeep sir do that helps a grieving young child?
qa.a: He named her sadness in simple words, stayed close, gave her a new crayon and kept the routine steady.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt watching Gunjan go from laughing to sobbing?
qa.a: Chaitanya may have been surprised and moved, not knowing what Gunjan felt inside but seeing how fast her mood changed.

grounding: A classroom helper sees a young girl back after a bereavement play normally, then sob over a broken crayon, and the teacher respond with simple words and routine.

passage:
Tuesday: Madhav came back to class after his Nani's funeral and zoomed his toy car around as if nothing had happened. Sumit sir let him.
Thursday: Madhav's crayon broke in half. He threw it and wailed, "It's broken! It's all broken!" Sumit sir sat beside him. "You feel very sad. Nani died, and that is very sad." Madhav leaned on his arm.
The next Monday: Madhav drew a house with a big sun. "That's Nani's house," he said, then ran off to the swings.

qa.q: What did Madhav do with his toy car on Tuesday?
qa.a: He zoomed his toy car around as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: What might Madhav's wail 'It's all broken!' show about his feelings?
qa.a: His grief about Nani may have come out through the broken crayon, a short burst of the big sadness he couldn't put into words.

qa.q: Which of Sumit sir's choices helps most at this stage?
qa.a: Using simple, honest words about Nani's death and sitting beside Madhav, while letting normal play and routine continue.

qa.q: How might Sumit sir feel when Madhav says 'That's Nani's house' and runs off?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and tender, seeing Madhav mention Nani calmly and then go back to play.

grounding: Over several days a teacher sees a young boy play as if nothing happened after a death, then cry over a crayon, and helps with simple words and routine.

passage: The courtyard in their village near Jorhat was full of relatives and the smell of incense when Aita's body was carried out. Alka, ten, sat on the steps with dry eyes. Everyone else was crying. She tugged her father's sleeve. 'Deuta, can I have some pitha? I'm hungry.' Bhupen stared at her, then nodded slowly and fetched a plate. Later she asked if she could watch cartoons on Mami's phone. A cousin whispered that Alka didn't even care. But when the cartoon ended, Alka didn't ask for another. She sat very still, holding the phone, looking at Aita's empty chair by the door, and didn't say a word until dark.

qa.q: What did Alka ask her father for?
qa.a: She asked for some pitha because she was hungry.

qa.q: Why might Alka seem so calm and ask for food and cartoons?
qa.a: The loss may be too big to take in at once, so her mind is keeping it at a distance; it doesn't mean she doesn't care.

qa.q: How could Bhupen support Alka at this stage?
qa.a: He could let her eat and rest without judging, stay near her, and gently tell her she can talk or cry whenever she's ready.

qa.q: Why is the cousin's whisper that Alka 'didn't even care' unfair?
qa.a: The cousin sees only her calm surface, not the stillness and silence by Aita's chair that suggest deep feeling held back.

grounding: After her grandmother's death a ten-year-old seems oddly calm, asks for food and cartoons, then falls silent as the feeling is held at a distance.

passage: The call from Enugu came on Saturday morning: Chidi's grandpa had died in the night. Mum cried in the kitchen of their Houston apartment. Chidi, nine, sat at the counter and asked, 'Can I still have pancakes?' Dad made them, slowly. When Jin knocked to ask if Chidi could play video games, Chidi said yes and played for an hour, laughing at the usual jokes. Jin didn't know yet. After Jin left, Chidi switched off the screen and sat on the sofa with Grandpa's last birthday card in his lap. He didn't open it. He didn't cry. He just stayed there, very quiet, until the light outside turned orange.

qa.q: Where did the call about Chidi's grandpa come from?
qa.a: The call came from Enugu.

qa.q: What might Chidi's playing and laughing, then sitting silently with the card, suggest?
qa.a: The loss seems too big to feel all at once; he held it at a distance while playing, and it began to come closer when he was alone.

qa.q: What might help Chidi now, as he sits quietly with the card?
qa.a: A parent sitting beside him without pushing, maybe saying 'We can open it together whenever you want,' so he knows he isn't alone with it.

qa.q: What might Jin feel on learning later what had happened that morning?
qa.a: Jin may be surprised Chidi seemed so normal, and perhaps unsure about having joked around, then glad to have kept him company.

grounding: A nine-year-old asks for pancakes and plays games after his grandfather's death, then goes quiet, as the loss is too big to feel at once.

passage: For the third night in a row, Hana asked the same question at bedtime in their Oslo flat. 'Pappa, where is Mormor now?' Anders gave the same answer: 'Mormor died. Her body stopped working, and she can't come back. We remember her.' Hana nodded. In the afternoons she lined up her stuffed animals, laid the rabbit in a shoebox and made the bear sing a slow song. Every Sunday at four, when Mormor used to arrive with cinnamon buns, Hana still ran to the window. 'Maybe she's late,' she said once. Anders didn't correct her sharply. He just sat with her by the glass until she turned away on her own.

qa.q: What did Mormor use to bring on Sundays at four?
qa.a: Mormor used to arrive with cinnamon buns.

qa.q: Why does Hana keep asking the same question every night?
qa.a: Hana is still confused and missing Mormor; repeating the question helps her slowly make the loss real, as each honest answer lets a little more sink in.

qa.q: What is Anders doing that helps Hana at this stage?
qa.a: He gives the same short, honest answer each time and sits with her at the window instead of scolding or distracting her.

qa.q: What might it be like for Anders to answer the same question night after night?
qa.a: It is probably painful, since the loss may be his too, yet he stays patient because he sees Hana needs it 🤍.

grounding: A grieving girl repeats the same question, acts out a funeral with toys and still watches for her grandmother, slowly making the loss real.

passage: In the Class 3 play corner, Siddharth had built a small stretcher from rulers and laid a toy soldier on it. He walked it slowly across the mat while two friends hummed. 'This is Nana's funeral,' he told Manoj sir, quite matter-of-fact. At lunch he asked again, 'Sir, where do people go when they die? Where did Nana go?' He had asked the same thing on Monday and Wednesday. And every day at the gate, he looked for Nana's blue scooter before remembering. Manoj sir crouched down each time. 'People believe different things about where we go. What does your family say?' Siddharth thought. 'Ma says he's in our hearts.' 'Then that's a good place to keep him.'

qa.q: What did Siddharth look for every day at the gate?
qa.a: He looked for Nana's blue scooter.

qa.q: What does Siddharth acting out Nana's funeral suggest he is doing inside?
qa.a: He seems sad and to be grieving Nana, replaying the funeral in play so that the loss slowly becomes real to him.

qa.q: Why is Manoj sir's answer about where people go a wise one?
qa.a: He is honest that beliefs differ and lets Siddharth bring his family's words, which respects the home's beliefs and still answers patiently.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's friends experience humming at the play funeral?
qa.a: They may treat it as an ordinary game or feel a little unsure, but joining in helps Siddharth feel less alone.

grounding: At school a grieving boy acts out his grandfather's funeral, repeats questions about where he went and still looks for him at the gate.

passage: In the school counsellor's small office, Abhinav's mother twisted the strap of her bag. 'Since his Nani died, he asks the same questions every night. Will you die? Will I die? Where is she? And yesterday I found him burying his toy car in a flowerpot and saying prayers. Is something wrong with him?' Mr Irfan, the counsellor, listened. 'This is very common. Repeating questions and playing it out is how children his age make sense of a loss. Short, honest answers help more than changing the subject.' He paused. 'If it keeps going or worries you, we can talk again, and the doctor too.' She let go of the strap. 'So I don't have to stop him?' 'You can just sit with him.'

qa.q: Where did Abhinav's mother find him burying his toy car?
qa.a: She found him burying it in a flowerpot.

qa.q: What does the mother twisting her bag strap suggest?
qa.a: She is anxious and afraid that her son's repeated questions and play mean something is wrong.

qa.q: What advice did Mr Irfan give, and why does it help?
qa.a: To give short, honest, patient answers rather than distract him, because repeating and playing is how children make sense of a loss.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel if his mother kept changing the subject instead?
qa.a: He might feel his questions are wrong or scary, and be left more alone and confused with his grief.

grounding: A mother worries about her grieving son's repeated questions and burial play, and a counsellor explains it is usually normal and honest answers help.

passage: I'm Sunaina, and I'm writing down what I've seen in Vikas since his Dadu died, because I'm scared I'm missing something. Every evening at seven, the time Dadu used to call, he checks my phone. Twice this week he asked, 'But where exactly is Dadu now?' I said, 'He died, beta. His body stopped, and he can't come back.' He nodded, then asked again the next day. Yesterday I saw him make a garland of paper flowers and lay it on Dadu's chair. I don't know what goes on in his head. At first I tried distracting him with cartoons. It didn't help. Now I just answer, simply, every time he asks. He seems calmer afterwards.

qa.q: What time does Vikas check his mother's phone every evening?
qa.a: At seven, the time Dadu used to call.

qa.q: Why is Sunaina scared, and what shows it?
qa.a: She worries his repeated questions and garland-making mean something is wrong; she even writes it all down in case she's missing something.

qa.q: Which approach seems to help Vikas more, and why?
qa.a: Answering simply and honestly every time, rather than distracting him with cartoons, because it lets him make sense of the loss and he seems calmer afterwards.

qa.q: What might Vikas be looking for when he checks the phone at seven?
qa.a: He may half-expect Dadu's call, a sign that he is still searching and slowly learning the calls won't come 🤍.

grounding: A mother records her grieving son's repeated questions and ritual play, fears it is unhealthy, and finds short honest answers help more than distraction.

passage:
Subject: sorry about yesterday
Sumit,
I know I yelled at you in the canteen. You only asked if I'd done the chemistry assignment and I told you to mind your own business in front of everyone. I haven't done it. I haven't done anything since Ma died. I come home, shut my door and lie there. Papa knocks and I say I'm studying.
The thing is, I'm not even angry at you. I'm angry that the doctors couldn't fix it, that Papa couldn't, that everyone keeps saying 'be strong' like it's a switch. Mostly I'm scared. Of what happens to us now. Of forgetting her voice.
Don't tell anyone. But don't give up on me either.
Mridul

qa.q: What had Sumit asked Mridul in the canteen?
qa.a: He only asked if Mridul had done the chemistry assignment.

qa.q: What feelings does Mridul reveal beneath his anger?
qa.a: Fear about what happens to his family now and of forgetting his mother's voice, along with helplessness that no one could fix it.

qa.q: What could help Mridul at this stage besides Sumit's friendship?
qa.a: Talking to a trusted adult, like his Papa or the school counsellor, so he isn't carrying the fear alone behind a closed door.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel reading this email?
qa.a: Probably relieved the anger wasn't really about him, and worried for Mridul, wanting to stay close while hoping he gets more support.

grounding: A teenager who lost his mother snaps at a friend, skips work and shuts his door, and admits fear and helplessness beneath the anger.

passage: You want to know why I've been such a monster, Gautam? Fine. Since Papa died in March, everything makes me furious. Kirti laughs too loud at lunch and I want to throw my tray. The class teacher says 'take your time with the syllabus' and I want to scream that time is exactly what we didn't have. I skipped two tests. I stay in my room with the door locked and headphones on, even when Ma knocks and says, 'Jaya, eat something.' Everyone says he's in a better place. Better than here? With us? I'm angry at the doctors, at everything, at the grown-ups who kept saying it'd be okay. And under all that... I'm scared. Of Ma crying at night. Of it happening again. There. Happy now?

qa.q: How many tests has Jaya skipped?
qa.a: She skipped two tests.

qa.q: What is Jaya really feeling beneath the fury?
qa.a: She's scared, of her mother crying at night and of losing someone again, and helpless because the adults couldn't keep their promise that it would be okay.

qa.q: What could Gautam do after hearing this?
qa.a: Stay with her without arguing, and gently encourage her to talk to her Ma or a school counsellor so she isn't alone with the fear.

qa.q: What might Jaya's Ma be going through when she knocks on the locked door?
qa.a: She is grieving too and probably worried and lonely, wanting to reach her daughter but not knowing how.

grounding: A teenage girl who lost her father snaps at friends, skips tests and locks her door, with fear and helplessness beneath her anger.

passage: I'm Tanvir, and I sit behind Damini in Class 10. For the first two weeks after her brother died, people were so careful. Teachers let her skip homework; the girls walked her to the bus. Then it stopped. Now it's six weeks later and nobody says his name. At lunch they talk about the fest and a new film, and Damini sits there with her tiffin closed. Yesterday someone laughed about a video, and she got up and left. I heard her say to herself on the stairs, 'Like he never existed.' I wanted to say something, but I was scared of making it worse, of making her cry. I think everyone is. I think that's the problem.

qa.q: How long after her brother died is it now?
qa.a: It's six weeks later.

qa.q: What does Damini's 'Like he never existed' reveal about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels alone and even betrayed, as if everyone has forgotten her brother while she is still grieving.

qa.q: What small step could Tanvir or the others take now?
qa.a: Gently say her brother's name or ask, 'Do you want to talk about him?', and let her choose; a trusted teacher or counsellor could also check in.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir think everyone has stopped mentioning the death?
qa.a: He believes they're scared that saying the name will hurt her more or make her cry, so their silence comes from fear, not forgetting.

grounding: A classmate sees a bereaved teenage girl feel alone and betrayed as others stop mentioning her brother, while they stay silent out of fear.

passage:
Week one after the rites. Anirban came every evening to Dolma's house in Darjeeling with notes from school and sat on the steps with her. Sometimes they talked about her Ama; sometimes they didn't talk at all.
Week five. Anirban stopped coming. At school he talked about football and exams, never about Ama. Dolma waited for him to ask how she was. He didn't. That night she wrote in her notebook: Even he's moved on.
Week seven. On the bus she finally asked him, voice shaking, 'Why don't you ever say her name?' Anirban looked at his hands. 'I thought if I did, you'd be sad again. I didn't want to be the one who made you cry.' Dolma stared at him. 'I'm already sad. Saying her name helps.'

qa.q: What did Anirban bring when he came in week one?
qa.a: He brought notes from school.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she wrote 'Even he's moved on'?
qa.a: She felt alone and betrayed, believing even her close friend had forgotten her Ama.

qa.q: What turning point happens on the bus, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Dolma asks why Anirban never says her mother's name and learns his silence came from fear; telling him that saying it helps lets them grieve together again.

qa.q: What had Anirban been afraid of all those weeks?
qa.a: He was afraid that mentioning her Ama would make Dolma sad again and that he'd be the one who made her cry 🤍.

grounding: Over weeks a bereaved teenage girl feels abandoned as her friend stops mentioning her mother, then learns he stayed silent out of fear.
